'''''Veronica serpyllifolia''''', the '''thyme-leaved speedwell'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''thymeleaf speedwell''',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/WEEDS/thymeleaf_speedwell.html|publisher=UC IPM|title=Thymeleaf speedwell (Veronica serpyllifolia)|access-date=2019-04-25}}</ref> is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the [[Plantaginaceae|plantain family]]. The species as a whole is native mostly to Eurasia & North America, and has three variants with their individual ranges; var. serpyllifolia has particularly spread beyond its native range.

==Description==

''Veronica serpyllifolia'' L. initially grows low to the ground then will start to grow upright.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Parnell | first1=John A. N. | last2=Cullen | first2=Elaine L. | last3=Webb | first3=D. A. | last4=Curtis | first4=Tom | title=Webb's An Irish Flora | publisher=Cork University Press | publication-place=Cork | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-909005-08-2 | oclc=830022856}}</ref> The leaves are borne on creeping stems. Roots grow from leaf axils.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Parnell | first1=John A. N. | last2=Cullen | first2=Elaine L. | last3=Webb | first3=D. A. | last4=Curtis | first4=Tom | title=Webb's An Irish Flora | publisher=Cork University Press | publication-place=Cork | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-909005-08-2 | oclc=830022856}}</ref> This plant can be hard to spot as it is relatively small and grows in patches which can be covered by grass. They are more noticeable when they bloom.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Veronica serpyllifolia (Thyme-leaf Speedwell): Minnesota Wildflowers|url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/thyme-leaf-speedwell|access-date=2021-11-17|website=www.minnesotawildflowers.info|language=en}}</ref> The prostrate stems bear erect flowering branches up to {{cvt|20|cm}} high.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Parnell | first1=John A. N. | last2=Cullen | first2=Elaine L. | last3=Webb | first3=D. A. | last4=Curtis | first4=Tom | title=Webb's An Irish Flora | publisher=Cork University Press | publication-place=Cork | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-909005-08-2 | oclc=830022856}}</ref>

The first leaves of the seedling have no petiole, are hairless, and have a smooth margin.<ref name="ipm.ucanr">{{Cite web|title=Weed Gallery: Thymeleaf speedwell|url=http://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/WEEDS/thymeleaf_speedwell.html|access-date=2021-11-18|website=ipm.ucanr.edu}}</ref> The leaves are oval, and the lower leaves have smooth margins. The upper leaves are smaller than the lower. The leaves are opposite, with the lower leaves having relatively short stalks, while the higher or upper leaves are stalkless (lack petioles).<ref name="ipm.ucanr">{{Cite web|title=Weed Gallery: Thymeleaf speedwell|url=http://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/WEEDS/thymeleaf_speedwell.html|access-date=2021-11-18|website=ipm.ucanr.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last1=Parnell | first1=John A. N. | last2=Cullen | first2=Elaine L. | last3=Webb | first3=D. A. | last4=Curtis | first4=Tom | title=Webb's An Irish Flora | publisher=Cork University Press | publication-place=Cork | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-909005-08-2 | oclc=830022856}}</ref>

The flowers are small, white, and have dark purple marks on their petals. They have four petals, and a corolla {{cvt|6|mm}} wide. They grow in racemes from the leaf axils.<ref name="Penn State">{{Cite web|title=Lawn and Turfgrass Weeds: Thyme-leaf Speedwell|url=https://extension.psu.edu/lawn-and-turfgrass-weeds-thyme-leaf-speedwell|access-date=2021-10-20|website=Penn State Extension|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last1=Parnell | first1=John A. N. | last2=Cullen | first2=Elaine L. | last3=Webb | first3=D. A. | last4=Curtis | first4=Tom | title=Webb's An Irish Flora | publisher=Cork University Press | publication-place=Cork | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-909005-08-2 | oclc=830022856}}</ref> Their stems grow from nodes on the rhizomes, allowing them to grow in thick mats close to the ground.<ref name="ipm.ucanr">{{Cite web|title=Weed Gallery: Thymeleaf speedwell|url=http://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/WEEDS/thymeleaf_speedwell.html|access-date=2021-11-18|website=ipm.ucanr.edu}}</ref>

''Veronica serpyllifolia'' reproduces either by dropping its seeds or by rooting stems. Their root systems are both fibrous and rhizomatous.<ref name="ipm.ucanr" /><ref name="illinoiswildflowers">{{Cite web|title=Thyme-Leaved Speedwell (Veronica serpyllifolia)|url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/th_speedwell.htm|access-date=2021-11-16|website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref> The fruits are obcordate (heart shaped) capsules, mostly flattened, and have a pubescent outer layer with a notched tip. They are approximately {{cvt|2.5-3.5|mm}} long.<ref name="ipm.ucanr" /> The fruit is lined with hairs and the seeds on the inside of the capsule are also flattened.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Veronica serpyllifolia (Thyme-leaf Speedwell): Minnesota Wildflowers|url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/thyme-leaf-speedwell|access-date=2021-11-17|website=www.minnesotawildflowers.info|language=en}}</ref> Once the capsules are mature, they open to release many small seeds.<ref name="illinoiswildflowers">{{Cite web|title=Thyme-Leaved Speedwell (Veronica serpyllifolia)|url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/th_speedwell.htm|access-date=2021-11-16|website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref>

== Distribution ==

''Veronica serpyllifolia'' L. var. serpyllifolia, commonly known as thyme-leaved speedwell, is native mostly to Eurasia and is introduced to North America and New Zealand.{{cn|date=July 2023}} As of 2010, it is known to occur in 37 of the US states and is considered a weed in North America. It frequently occurs in open grass lands and cultivated areas on lighter soils.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2017|title=Anthecology of Veronica serpyllifolia subsp. serpyllifolia (Plantaginaceae) in Moscow region.|journal=Растительный Мир Азиатской России |script-journal=ru:Растительный мир Азиатской России|issue=4|doi=10.21782/rmar1995-2449-2017-4(42-46) |issn=1995-2449}}</ref>  It grows in full sunlight, tolerates partial shade, and thrives in a moist environment during the spring.<ref name="illinoiswildflowers"/> It can grow at elevations up to {{cvt|3300|m}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Veronica serpyllifolia - FNA|url=http://beta.floranorthamerica.org/Veronica_serpyllifolia|access-date=2021-11-18|website=beta.floranorthamerica.org}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
Pollinators of ''V. serpyllifolia'' include flies and bees that visit the flowers for nectar.  The seeds can be dispersed by attaching onto the wings of birds or the fur of some animals. ''Veronica serpyllifolia'' seeds were found in cattle dung, thus cattle or other grazers are likely important dispersers of the plant.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Welch|first=D.|date=August 1985|title=Studies in the Grazing of Heather Moorland In North-East Scotland. IV. Seed Dispersal and Plant Establishment in Dung|journal=The Journal of Applied Ecology|volume=22|issue=2|pages=461–472|doi=10.2307/2403178|jstor=2403178|bibcode=1985JApEc..22..461W |issn=0021-8901}}</ref> 

== Weed control ==
''Veronica serpyllifolia'' grows in patches and is commonly recognized as a weed of turf grass. Ways to remove ''V. serpyllifolia'' from lawns are by mowing and watering and fertilizing lawns properly, this hinders the weeds ability to compete.<ref name="illinoiswildflowers" /> The use of herbicide is recommended for the complete removal of this species from a yard or a lawn. Picking the weed and pulling the roots out can work but this risks the further dispersal of seeds on the lawn.<ref name="Penn State"/> One study showed that wiping herbicides onto the plant rather than spraying it helps to better remove of the species. It stated that wiping method worked better and the spray on method caused harm to other grasses surrounding the weeds.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Harrington|first1=K. C.|last2=Hood|first2=M. Z.|last3=McKinnon|first3=K. C.|date=2000-08-01|title=Assessment of two herbicide wiping devices|url=https://nzpps.org/_journal/index.php/nzpp/article/view/3707|journal=New Zealand Plant Protection|language=en|volume=53|pages=273–276|doi=10.30843/nzpp.2000.53.3707|issn=1179-352X|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Synonyms ==
Synonyms of ''Veronica serpyllifolia'' include: ''Veronicastrum serpyllifolium (L.)'' Fourr. and ''Veronica serpyllifolia L. var. nummularioides'' Lecoq & Lamotte.<ref name="USDA Plants Database">{{Cite PLANTS |symbol=VESE |taxon=''Veronica serpyllifolia'' |access-date=2021-11-16}}</ref>

== Wetland plant status ==
''Veronica serpyllifolia'' is able to grow in both jurisdictional wetlands and non-wetlands.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Veronica serpyllifolia ssp. humifusa Calflora|url=https://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=8255|access-date=2021-11-17|website=www.calflora.org}}</ref> According to the wetland plant classification system in the United States, ''V. serpyllifolia'' is classified as a facultative (FAC) to obligate (OBL) wetland plant.<ref>{{Cite web|title=NWPL Home v3.4-f9c|url=https://cwbi-app.sec.usace.army.mil/nwpl_static/v34/home/home.html|access-date=2021-12-08|website=cwbi-app.sec.usace.army.mil}}{{dead link|date=April 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>
